subject: octopus
reasoning:
I'm planning the design for a TypeScript octopus model: a mantle on top with eyes, eight arms with suckers radiating outward and splayed along the floor, sized roughly 0.6m across with a 0.25m mantle and 0.5m arms, facing forward.

Now I'm working out the skeleton structure — a body joint with mantle and head, then eight arm chains curving outward and downward to lie flat on the floor, with radius tapering from thick at the base to thin at the tip, keeping each arm's centerline just touching the ground without clipping through it. I'm defining each arm's path using radial distance and angle around the Y-axis, adding a slight sideways wiggle for a natural splayed rest pose.

Working out point coordinates...

Now I'm setting up the chain of arm joints attached to the body, naming them sequentially, and sweeping a tube along each arm's curve with a radius function, using a mottled countershaded color for the skin.

For suckers, I'm placing small disc shapes along the underside of each arm at specific angles facing outward and downward, generating two staggered rows down the length using simple cylinder geometry.

Angling the underside suckers slightly off the bottom-center looks more natural, and now I'm sketching the mantle as a tilted sweep chain from the base up and back, working out the radius profile for a rounded bulb shape.

Setting the body's lowest sweep point so its rounded bottom just barely clears the floor, and starting the arm chains a bit above that with a smaller radius so they tuck neatly inside the mantle wall rather than poking out.

Now I'm placing the eyes on the front-lower part of the mantle using angular coordinates around a reference point, bulging them out as small gold spheres attached to the surface, then adding flattened pupil shapes stuck onto each eye to give them a slit-like look.

Adding an eyelid using a flattened torus ring oriented along the surface normal and embedded slightly into the body, then I'm planning a small siphon funnel spike near the lower front-right of the body.

I'm scattering knobby papillae spheres across the mantle for texture, then adding a beak structure underneath with separate upper and lower jaw joints positioned near the body's underside.

Adjusting beak tip placement to keep it subtle, then thinking about webbing between arms—I'll use membrane connections between adjacent arm chains near their base, slicing the path to cover only a partial length so the web doesn't stretch unnaturally across the full arm.

I'll skip the membrane idea entirely—too risky and likely to look messy with the arm geometry. Better to keep things clean and instead focus on making the mantle larger and giving the arms a nice curl, with a splayed rest pose.

Now I'm setting up the color palette: orange-red base, dark shadow, pale underside, pink suckers, and gold eyes. For the skin, I'm layering countershading over mottled spots to give the body and arms natural texture, with the underside paling out appropriately. For the mantle, I'm building a curved path through control points to define its sweep.

Defining the mantle chain and sweep geometry...

Working out sucker geometry...

Checking the sucker geometry stays positive so nothing clips below the surface, then confirming the chain skeleton uses five spans matching the six-point path. Now I'm computing the curling tip pose with symmetric angles around the center for the wiggle motion.

Working out the radius taper and tip lift values, and adjusting arm base radius so it blends smoothly into the body. I'm checking that the overall footprint radius and arm spread feel proportionate to a real octopus scale.

Now I'm setting up the eye geometry — sinking a small sphere into the surface with an embed offset, then computing a ray from the eye's center along its normal axis to place the pupil correctly facing outward.

I'm also adding a thin torus ring around the eye socket for definition, and scattering small sphere papillae across upper body regions using filtered random points based on normal direction and height.

Now I'm setting up the beak geometry, placing a cone on the body for the upper beak pointed downward, and defining a jaw joint for the lower beak attachment.
